summary: Research for the GPU version of the Stage 1 presolve cascade, read-only. I read 14 web sources through the fetch tool (PaPILO paper and three of its source files, the two papers of Sofranac, Gleixner and Pokutta, the two GPU LP presolve papers of 2026, the PSLP paper, the distributed presolve paper of Kempke and others, Blelloch and others on deterministic reservations and on greedy maximal independent sets, Kelley and Rajamanickam, the CCCL determinism pages, cuOpt PR 2372 and PR 372), cuOpt's GPU bound propagation and probing files in the worktree, and the HiGHS presolve at commit 283bfc8. Main results: (1) two GPU presolvers for LP exist since 2026 (cuPSLP, 11 and 42 times faster than its CPU version on two LP sets; GPU-Preprocessor of HPR-LP, 6 to 44 times faster than PSLP), both LP only, both with floating-point atomics and no statement on reproducibility, so neither meets the owner's determinism rule as built; (2) PaPILO's scheme (compute on a frozen state, apply in a fixed order with a conflict check) is deterministic but its sequential apply phase and conflicts limit it to 1.9 times on all instances at 32 threads, and delayed application needs 62% more rounds than immediate application; (3) GPU bound propagation in Jacobi form is 7.4 times faster than a sequential code on a V100 over 786 instances without transfers, needs 1.4 times the rounds on average and up to 22 times, and loses to a marked sequential code after single bound changes; cuOpt's load-balanced kernels are not compiled in this tree, sum in an order that differs from the host, have no infinite-term counts and lose the single-infinity case; (4) deterministic reservations with an integer write-minimum give the sequential greedy result in parallel, but index order can need one round per element on chains, hashed priorities need about 8 to 14 rounds; (5) CCCL guarantees the same sum across GPU types only for the plain reduction, not for the segmented one; (6) in today's host engine on the 240 instances 47% of the time is outside the rules and about 42% is in first calls of the families, about 10% in later calls, and the longest cascade (unitcal_7) spends 24 microseconds of host time per family call, which is below the cost of one device primitive. Nobody seems to have built a GPU presolve for MIP rules, a bit-reproducible GPU presolve, or one with a host/device split inside a run.
report:
RESEARCH REPORT: what is known about parallel and GPU presolve, and what of it the Stage 1 cascade can use

0. WHAT I DID AND HOW FAR IT GOES

- Web: 20 searches and 27 page fetches. No query held the project's name, the owner's name or a path. Every web page was read through the fetch tool, which returns the answer of a small model on the page text, not the page. For three papers (PaPILO, Sofranac et al. 2022, cuPSLP) I made a second pass that asked for verbatim sentences and table rows, and the numbers agreed. The other sources had one pass (GPU-Preprocessor two passes with different questions). Section numbers below are those the tool returned.
- Two PDFs could not be read by the fetch tool. The tool stored both by itself in its own cache (/Users/acoerduek/.claude/projects/-Users-acoerduek-Documents-workspace-cuopt-wt-cuopt-b/c660eb6b-7edc-4afc-bf62-0442cb32d870/tool-results/webfetch-1795864703043-93mmlj.pdf and webfetch-1795864891598-fiv2xr.pdf). I did not save any file from the web myself. For the second one (Blelloch et al., PPoPP 2012) I extracted the text from the cache with a 60-line script, read it and deleted the text again.
- Local: read in full /Users/acoerduek/Documents/workspace/cuopt-wt/gpu-presolve/cpp/src/presolve/bounds_presolve.cu (368 lines), bounds_update_helpers.cuh (403), load_balanced_bounds_presolve_kernels.cuh (639), load_balanced_bounds_presolve.cu (700), load_balanced_partition_helpers.cuh (279); parts of probing_cache.cu, multi_probe.cu, lb_probing_cache.cu, load_balanced_bounds_presolve.cuh; in HiGHS (commit 283bfc8) the parts of highs/presolve/HPresolve.cpp named in section 5 and heads of HPresolveDualFixing.cpp and HPresolveParallelRowsAndCols.cpp; in the engine the heads of rules_parallel_rows.cpp, rules_propagation.cpp, hash.cpp, the driver's comments, DESIGN.md sections 2 and 3; and the stored run /Users/acoerduek/Documents/workspace/cuopt-wt/gpu-presolve/gpu_presolve/results/bench240/s1c_m1/release_all/summary.json (240 instances, identity commit daa4f5d68, 3 repetitions), from which I computed the tables of section 6.
- Path correction: the task names cpp/src/mip_heuristics/presolve. That directory does not exist in the worktree. The files are in /Users/acoerduek/Documents/workspace/cuopt-wt/gpu-presolve/cpp/src/presolve (moved by commit fdde8209c, "Move presolve from mip_heuristics to src/presolve (#2215)").
- Nothing was built or run except three small Python reads of summary.json. No file under the worktree was changed.

1. PaPILO

Read: Gleixner, Gottwald, Hoen, "PaPILO: A Parallel Presolving Library for Integer and Linear Optimization with Multiprecision Support", arXiv 2206.10709v3, sections 2.1 to 2.5 and the experiments; source on GitHub (scipopt/papilo, main): src/papilo/core/Presolve.hpp, src/papilo/core/ProblemUpdate.hpp (first 100,000 of 117,374 characters), src/papilo/presolvers/ParallelRowDetection.hpp, src/papilo/presolvers/ConstraintPropagation.hpp.

How it is parallel
- All presolvers of one round run in parallel on a read-only problem (Presolve.hpp, run_presolvers: tbb::parallel_for over the presolver indices, each writes into its own reductions[i]). Paper 2.2: "Each presolver has read-only access to the data."
- Reductions are grouped into transactions that carry their premises as lock reductions. ProblemUpdate.hpp, checkTransactionConflicts: a column lock conflicts if the column carries the state kModified, a column bounds lock if it carries kBoundsModified, a row lock if the row carries kModified or kBoundsModified. applyTransaction returns kRejected on a conflict, kPostponed for substitutions and sparsify entries while postponing is on, kInfeasible, or applies.
- Application is sequential: apply_all_presolver_reductions walks the presolvers in index order (stable sort by timing class, insertion order inside a class), then flushChangedCoeffs, then the postponed substitutions, then one flush. The state flags are cleared through the dirty lists (clearStates).
- The only parallel construct in ProblemUpdate.hpp is tbb::parallel_invoke in compress() (about ten independent array compactions).
- Round classes (addDefaultPresolvers): fast = singleton columns, coefficient strengthening, propagation; medium = fix continuous, simple probing, parallel rows, parallel columns, singleton stuffing, dual fixing, simplify inequalities, doubleton equations, clique merging; exhaustive = implied integers, dominated columns, dual inference, probing, substitution, sparsify. A round that changes little escalates fast -> medium -> exhaustive (abort factors per class); a round that changes enough restarts at fast.
- Inside a presolver: probing, dominated columns, sparsify and the row and column hashes are parallel; propagation, coefficient tightening, dual fixing, implied integers, simple probing, doubleton equations and simplify inequalities can be made parallel over rows or columns by parameters (paper 2.5). ConstraintPropagation.hpp: the parallel path (option constraint_propagation_parallel) runs tbb::parallel_for over the rows of changedactivities, each row writes into its own stored_reductions[j], and a sequential loop then emits them in list order. The presolver reads const bounds and activities and never writes them back, so a call is Jacobi-like: a row does not see a bound another row found in the same call.
- Parallel rows (ParallelRowDetection.hpp): a support id per row (hash of the index sequence, exact compare by memcmp, sequential), a coefficient hash after scaling by the first coefficient (tbb::parallel_for), a sort by (support id, coefficient hash, random row permutation), buckets of equal keys, every row of a bucket compared against the first row only, all rows of a group locked in one transaction.

Determinism
- Paper: "Regardless of the number of threads used all runs return the same reductions and hence the same presolved problem", because reductions "are stored and applied always in the same order". The sequential mode that applies each presolver's result at once (apply_results_immediately_if_run_sequentially) is a different process with a different result.

What limits the speedup (paper, MIPLIB 2017 collection, 1,022 instances with two seeds = 2,044 runs)
- Shifted geometric mean of presolve time (shift 1 s), threads 1 / 2 / 4 / 8 / 16 / 32: all 2,044 runs 0.74 / 0.57 / 0.48 / 0.42 / 0.40 / 0.39 s (1.9 times at 32 threads); the 134 runs of at least 10 s: 54.87 / 30.94 / 20.34 / 14.79 / 11.83 / 10.23 s (5.4 times); the 49 runs of at least 100 s: 7.0 times. 1,617 of the 2,044 runs take less than one second on one thread.
- The sequential application and state update are the fixed part; the authors place the 10 s subset slightly above the 20% sequential curve of Amdahl's law. "parallelizing (too) small chunks of work may even result in a performance decrease"; simple probing is not made parallel over all constraints because its checks are very fast.
- Conflicts (240 MIPLIB 2017 benchmark instances): "Only 16 of the 71 pairings cause conflicts". Singleton columns conflict with themselves on 27.7% of their transactions; doubleton equations lose 96,660 transactions (17.4%); dominated columns lose 46,789 of 128,069 (36.5%); substitution loses 108,607 and sparsify 6,965, mostly to themselves.
- Delayed against immediate application on one thread (990 instances): 23.53 against 14.54 rounds, that is 38% fewer rounds with immediate application (62% more with delayed), 0.73 s against 0.78 s, 56,803 against 56,258 nonzeros.

Usable, and how
- The scheme itself is what DESIGN.md section 3 calls the reservation table: candidates proved on a frozen state, each with the rows and columns its proof read, applied in one fixed order with a conflict check. It gives determinism for any degree of parallelism. Its price is known from the numbers above: more rounds, and rules whose candidates collide with their own kind (singleton columns, doubleton equations, dominated columns) lose a fifth to a third of a batch.
- Two premise classes are enough in PaPILO: "entries of the line changed" and "bounds or sides of the line changed", kept as flags with a dirty list. The same two bits per row and per column are cheap on a device.
- PaPILO's sequential apply phase is the part a GPU design must replace; PaPILO gives no parallel apply.

2. GPU DOMAIN PROPAGATION

2a. Sofranac, Gleixner, Pokutta, "Accelerating domain propagation: an efficient GPU-parallel algorithm over sparse matrices" (arXiv 2009.07785, Parallel Computing 109, 2022). Read: sections 2 to 5 (first 100,000 of 110,287 characters).
- One round = activities of all rows (a modified CSR-adaptive product: rows blocked, a "CSR-stream" kernel for many short rows, a "CSR-vector" kernel with one warp or all warps of a block for long rows), then one thread per nonzero computes a bound candidate. Candidates that improve on the bound of the previous round are written with atomic minimum and maximum on doubles (section 3.5: "we use CUDA's atomic operations to update bounds"). All threads see the bounds of the previous round, so the round is Jacobi-like; the sequential reference marks rows and uses new bounds at once.
- Rounds (section 2.2, 893 instances): 3.1 on average for the sequential code, 4.4 for the parallel one; the largest increase on one instance is 22 times; a chain of m constraints needs m rounds.
- Infinite terms (section 3.4): the infinite contributions to the minimum and the maximum activity are counted next to the finite sum, with integer reductions over data already loaded; with exactly one infinite term the residual of that column is finite and is used; with two or more no candidate.
- Loop (section 3.7): a host loop that reads one flag per round is faster overall than a loop kernel with dynamic parallelism and than one "megakernel" with grid synchronisation. The cap is 100 rounds; 30 of 987 instances do not converge within it.
- Results are compared with tolerances (1e-8 absolute, 1e-5 relative) against the sequential code, not bit by bit; the order of sums is not discussed. In single precision 27 of 987 instances reach a different point and 118 hit the cap.
- Numbers (double precision, 786 MIPLIB 2017 instances with at least 1,000 rows and columns, speedup over the authors' sequential code on a Xeon, data transfer and set-up not counted): V100 7.42, TITAN 2.98, RTX super 3.19, P400 0.47 in the geometric mean; by size class on the V100 2.35 (Set-1, 270 smallest instances), 12.93 (Set-4), 43.92 (Set-8, 36 largest); 95th percentile 51.65; up to 180 on single instances (abstract). Their OpenMP code reaches 1.10 (8 threads, i7), 0.14 (24 threads, Xeon), 0.04 (64 threads). The V100 is faster than the sequential code on about 93% of the instances.
- Section 5: after a single bound change (branching) the sequential code "can in most cases avail of the constraint marking mechanism" and is often faster.

2b. Sofranac, Gleixner, Pokutta, "An algorithm-independent measure of progress for linear constraint propagation" (arXiv 2106.07573, CP 2021). Read: sections 2 to 5.
- The fixed point is unique but may not be reached in finite time. Progress is measured separately for bounds that become finite and for finite bounds, relative to the limit point.
- 540 instances, V100 against a Xeon Gold 6246: at the fixed point the GPU code is 4.9 times faster in finite reductions and 5.4 times in infinite-to-finite reductions; the speedup peaks near 50% progress (7.8 and 7.0) and drops steeply in the last few percent. No stopping rule is recommended; criteria on local progress are called reasonable.

2c. cuOpt's own code (read locally, not run)
- Compiled today: bounds_presolve.cu with bounds_update_helpers.cuh. One block of 256 threads per row (bounds_presolve.cu lines 100-102), each thread sums a strided share of the row and cub::BlockReduce adds the shares (bounds_update_helpers.cuh lines 125-136); one block per column takes the maximum and minimum of the candidates of its rows (lines 318-345); rounds are Jacobi-like; one read-back of an integer per round (bounds_presolve.cu line 126); changed rows and columns are marked with atomicExch on integers (lines 132, 343), the change count with an integer atomicAdd (line 235). The residual is formed by subtracting the own term from the activity (lines 196-197). There are no infinite-term counts: an infinite bound enters as a product.
- Load-balanced version (load_balanced_bounds_presolve.cu, _kernels.cuh, _helpers.cuh, load_balanced_partition_helpers.cuh): rows and columns are binned by ceil(log2(length)); lengths up to 16 share a warp (1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 threads per row, kernels.cuh lines 18-40 and 287-353), longer ones get a block, lines above 16 * 1024 entries (load_balanced_bounds_presolve.cuh line 141) are split over several blocks and combined by a second kernel (kernels.cuh lines 67-142). The kernel sequence is a CUDA graph launched with one call per half round, with the read-back of the change count as a copy node of the graph (load_balanced_bounds_presolve.cu lines 345-453, 494-526). The row kernel stores the slack (side minus activity), and writes NaN into the slack of an infeasible row as a marker (kernels.cuh lines 94-105, 379).
- Not compiled: no CMakeLists.txt under cpp/src or cpp/tests names a load_balanced or lb_ file (cpp/src/presolve/CMakeLists.txt lines 26-35 list bounds_presolve.cu, multi_probe.cu, probing_cache.cu). That PR 372 is the cause I could not confirm: the page of NVIDIA/cuopt PR 372 ("Combined variable bounds", merged 2025-09-10) does not say so.
- What the load-balanced kernels lack against the owner's rules, by reading: (i) the sum order is strided threads plus a library tree and depends on the bin and the block size, so it differs from the host's order, and it is not compensated; (ii) no infinite-term counts; with one infinite term the candidate of the column that holds it is infinity minus infinity (kernels.cuh lines 388-389) and is dropped, which is the loss PR 2372 describes (x1 + x2 + x3 <= 10 with x3 free gives no bound on x3); that the NaN is dropped by the maximum is my reading of the device max function, not tested; (iii) NaN is also the marker of an infeasible row; (iv) the acceptance rule is "changed by more than 1000 absolute tolerances" (lines 408-414); (v) binning places a row inside its bin with an atomic counter (partition_helpers.cuh lines 126-139), so the storage order inside a bin can differ between runs; each row's own sum is not affected.
- Liftable: the binning by length, the warp-shared kernels for short lines, the split of very long lines, the slack array read by the column kernel (no candidate array of nonzero size), the CUDA graph with the read-back inside it, and the column-wise reduction by maximum and minimum, which is exact in any order and needs no floating-point atomic (the paper of 2a uses floating-point atomics for this step; cuOpt does not).
- cuOpt PR 2372 (open, author gtjusila, "Fix GPU bound propagation for rows with a single infinite activity term"): the review comments match the owner's constraints: counts as uint16_t in separate arrays ("I don't think there are rows that are larger than uint16, and even if that's the case, we can just skip them"), no second block reduction ("I am worried about doubling the reductions"; count per thread and one integer atomicAdd only if nonzero), tests with INTEGER variables, a benchmark against regressions. An automatic review comment on the same PR says the single-infinity candidate can pass a feasible point through rounding in the finite sum and asks for an error bound or a rejection; DESIGN.md 2.4 already has an error guard for this.
- Probing (probing_cache.cu, multi_probe.cu): a host OpenMP loop over integer variables sorted by a priority computed on the device; each thread owns a propagation object that runs two probes in one kernel pass (two bound sets in calc_activity_kernel and update_bounds, bounds_update_helpers.cuh lines 53-110 and 242-307); results are copied to the host per variable; bound changes are queued per thread and applied after each step in a fixed order, and the work count is folded in task order so that it is the same for any thread count (probing_cache.cu, about lines 1005-1020). This is Stage 2 material; the pattern (a step on a frozen state, a fixed-order apply) is the same as PaPILO's.

Usable, and how
- A Jacobi sweep with row activities, exact infinite-term counts and a column-wise maximum and minimum is the proven device form, and it is deterministic if the row sum has one fixed order. Expect 1.4 times the sweeps of a Gauss-Seidel host pass on average and far more on chains. The measured fact of the project (the first call holds 92.5% of the propagation work on 17 local instances) and section 5 of the paper point the same way: the first full sweeps on the device, the marked tail on the host.
- The host loop with one read-back per round is the better loop (paper 3.7), which fits the local cost of 13.8 microseconds per read-back.

3. GPU AND PARALLEL PRESOLVE BEYOND THAT

3a. cuPSLP: Cederberg and Boyd, "GPU-Accelerated Presolving for Linear Programming", arXiv 2609.16182 (14 Sep 2026). Read: all sections, two passes. Source code: not found.
- LP only. "The two presolvers implement the same set of explorers" as PSLP, that is (PSLP paper, Table 1): singleton rows, doubleton rows, redundant constraints, singleton columns in equations and in inequalities, lock-based dual fixing, parallel rows, parallel columns, primal propagation, dual propagation. "All the explorers and reductions of cuPSLP are implemented on the GPU"; postsolve runs on the CPU; the postsolve stack is kept on the GPU and "flush[ed] to the host as it approaches its capacity".
- Propagation (3.1): one fused kernel per row class, "one thread to each short row, one warp to each medium row, and one block to each long row"; "Because the bounds are updated in place (using atomic operations), a tightening made during a round is seen immediately", "effectively of Gauss-Seidel type"; rounds until nothing changes "or after a small fixed number of rounds". Load balancing chosen per instance is 2.3 times faster in the median than the best fixed scheme on the 21 GAMS instances; one instance has a row of 2.4 million entries, 8% of its nonzeros.
- Matrix (3.2): A and its transpose in CSR; "Rather than physically removing an eliminated variable from A, we mark it as inactive"; only line sizes and inactive flags are maintained; activities and locks are recomputed before the explorers that need them, not updated.
- Parallel rows (3.2): a two-level hash, one warp per row; inside a hash group every row is compared with a leader (the first equation, else the first inequality). Parallel columns are parallel rows of the transpose with the cost row. Singleton columns: one thread per column; the substitution into the objective is deferred for long rows and run as tasks of one block each.
- What the paper does not say: how reductions that touch the same row or column in one pass are resolved, how doubleton substitutions with fill-in are applied, when the matrix is compacted, anything on reproducibility.
- Numbers: Xeon Gold 6338 against an A100, transfers not counted, shifted geometric mean (shift 1 s): 49 Mittelmann LP instances 0.581 s against 0.051 s (11 times), 21 GAMS instances 30.4 s against 0.73 s (42 times); reduced sizes "similar" except two instances. One GPU thread is about 1,000 times slower than one CPU core for sequential work: summing 2.4 million doubles "takes 174 ms on a single A100 thread, versus 175 microseconds on a single Apple M4 Pro core" (2.2).
- Section 5: removing linearly dependent equations "seems inherently difficult to parallelize"; "A natural presolve design is therefore hybrid: move the relevant equality constraints to the CPU".

3b. GPU-Preprocessor of HPR-LP: Chen, Lu, Sun, Yuan, Zhang, Zhang, Zhao, "GPU-Accelerated Preprocessing for Large-Scale Linear Programming", arXiv 2610.19840 (14 Oct 2026). Read: first 100,000 of 110,969 characters, two passes.
- LP only. Rules: fixed and infeasible variables, redundant and infeasible rows, empty lines, singleton rows, bound strengthening, singleton columns, dual fixing, doubleton equations, parallel rows and columns, column domination for set covering, two special rules, plus "folding" (a randomised partition refinement by products with random vectors).
- Phases (3.1, 3.3.1): start-up; clean-up (fixed variables, empty lines, singleton rows and columns, repeated until nothing changes); propagation (bound strengthening, redundant rows, dual fixing); aggregation (doubleton equations); parallel detection. Clean-up runs after every phase that made progress; a limit K caps the phase runs.
- Updates (3.3.2): "Scan-Plan-Apply": kernels scan with deletion masks, record deletions and vector updates in a shared plan, and one apply step rebuilds A and its transpose once per batch. Doubleton equations: "candidate equations are detected in parallel. A subset of equations that do not share variables is then selected for batched substitution on the GPU"; "Changes to row bounds are summed using atomic operations when substitutions affect the same row". The selection method, the handling of chains and reproducibility are not described.
- Parallel rows and columns: signatures from a product with random vectors, groups by hashed indices and scaled values, exact test inside a group.
- Numbers (one H100, transfers not counted, shifted geometric mean with shift 10): preprocessing 6.0 to 43.9 times faster than PSLP and 23.2 to 677.7 times faster than Gurobi's presolve over three sets (49 Mittelmann LPs, 18 MIPLIB LP relaxations above 1e7 nonzeros, 20 QAP LPs); mean time on the 18 MIPLIB relaxations 0.292 s against 3.214 s (PSLP) and 9.903 s (Gurobi). Remaining nonzeros on those 18: 0.342 against 0.608 (PSLP) and 0.525 (Gurobi); folding alone gives 0.454, so the lead is not from the classical rules alone.

3c. PSLP: Cederberg and Boyd, "Presolving for GPU-Accelerated First-Order LP Solvers", arXiv 2604.23951. Read: one pass.
- A C presolver, mostly one thread, CSR and CSC with spare space per line, work lists of rows to revisit. On 48 Mittelmann instances and 383 MIPLIB 2017 LP relaxations (above 1e5 nonzeros) it is 11.8 and 6.58 times faster than Gurobi's presolve and reaches about 90% and 94% of its nonzero reduction. PSLP's time is 39.1% of the solve time of cuPDLPx on the MIPLIB relaxations above 1e7 nonzeros (Table 4). Section 1 of that paper still called a GPU presolve "rarely justified" and expected a modest gain; the same authors' cuPSLP reversed that five months later. It also notes that the GPU propagation paper runs up to 100 rounds while PSLP and Gurobi visit each constraint once per round.

3d. Kempke, Maher, Rehfeldt, Gleixner, Koch, Uslu, "Distributed Parallel Structure-Aware Presolving for Arrowhead Linear Programs", arXiv 2603.03498. Read: first 100,000 of 128,957 characters.
- Local reductions inside a block need no communication; changes to linking rows and columns are buffered and exchanged at synchronisation points; each process keeps its own postsolve stack with synchronisation events.
- Reproducibility (4.2): "we enforce a fixed order of the reduction operations within MPI collectives"; the result is deterministic for a fixed process count; between 64 processes and the maximum the presolved problems differ on 8 of 81 instances by at most 0.01% of the nonzeros. The fixed order costs time on five instances with 1,460 blocks (219 to 494 s against 37 to 87 s).
- 19 times faster than PaPILO and 6 times faster than Gurobi's presolve at 64 processes on 82 instances; on these instances Gurobi's presolve was observed to be "essentially sequential" although 128 threads were allowed.

3e. Commercial solvers. I found no publication, release note or talk that describes a parallel presolve in Gurobi, Xpress or COPT (three searches; the Xpress release notes in the results mention parallel root heuristics, not presolve). The only statement is the observation of 3d. This is an absence of evidence from a short search, not a finding.

3f. HiGHS: the presolve files hold no threading construct (search for parallel, spawn, TaskGroup, atomic use in highs/presolve). For LP only it has a separate first sweep (HPresolveInitialSweep, called at HPresolve.cpp about line 3995 when mipsolver == nullptr).

Usable, and how
- Both GPU presolvers confirm the matrix handling of DESIGN.md 2.3: flags and tombstones during a batch, a rebuild of the transpose once per batch, no dynamic structure.
- Both leave conflict resolution and the order of floating-point updates open or solve them with atomics. Their speed figures therefore do not include the cost of the owner's determinism rule.
- The phase scheme of 3b (a cheap clean-up cascade after every wide phase) is the same shape as DESIGN.md section 3.

4. BUILDING BLOCKS

4a. Deterministic reservations. Blelloch, Fineman, Gibbons, Shun, "Internally deterministic parallel algorithms can be fast", PPoPP 2012, sections 5.2 and 5.3, Table 2 (read from the cached PDF).
- A greedy loop over iterates in priority order is run in rounds. Each round takes a prefix of the remaining iterates; in a reserve phase every iterate writes its priority into the slots of the data it would touch with a write-minimum; in a commit phase an iterate that still holds its slots is executed; the rest are packed, in order, for the next round. "as long as the operations commute within the reserve and commit phases and the prefix size is selected deterministically, the computation is internally deterministic (the same iterates always fail)". For spanning forest it "will return the exact same spanning forest as the sequential algorithm". A prefix that is too large makes many iterates fail and repeat; one iterate is the sequential loop.
- Cost: on one thread the deterministic maximal independent set takes 0.782 s against 0.501 s for the sequential code (1.56 times) and reaches 0.054 s on 32 cores with hyper-threading; spanning forest 6.016 s against 2.653 s on one thread (2.27 times) and 0.326 s in parallel (Table 2, the paper's graphs).
- Blelloch, Fineman, Shun, "Greedy sequential maximal independent set and matching are parallel on average" (arXiv 1202.3205, sections 1, 3, 4, 6): the parallel greedy algorithm returns the same set as the sequential one for the same order; for a random order the number of rounds is O(log^2 n) with high probability (Theorem 3.5); for an arbitrary order the problem is P-complete, so no such bound exists; it is 4 to 8 times faster than their Luby implementation.
- My inference for the device: the write-minimum of a candidate number into a slot per row and per column is an integer atomic minimum, which the owner's rules allow, and its result does not depend on thread timing. It replaces a sort plus reduce-by-key (94 to 501 microseconds for a sort of 1e3 to 1e5 elements in the Stage 0 measurements) by one kernel. If the candidate number is the index, the result is the one of the host's sequential loop in index order, but a chain of candidates in index order (a path of doubleton equations, a staircase) commits one candidate per round. This follows from the algorithm and is not measured on the project's instances.

4b. Independent sets with hashed priorities. Kelley and Rajamanickam, "Parallel, Portable Algorithms for Distance-2 Maximal Independent Set and Graph Coarsening" (arXiv 2204.02934, sections III, V, VI).
- Each vertex gets a tuple (status, hash of round and vertex id, id) packed into one integer; a vertex whose tuple is the minimum of its neighbourhood enters the set; work lists are compacted by a scan between rounds. New priorities every round break chains. The result is "identical ... for a given input across all of these platforms" (two CPU and two GPU types). Rounds: 8 to 12 with their hash, 11 to 14 with priorities fixed once, on 17 matrices of 0.5 to 1.5 million vertices; 5 to 7 times faster than CUSP on a V100. Luby's algorithm (not read; described there as the distance-1 analogue) has O(log n) expected rounds.
- Usable: a rule for a batch that is deterministic on every machine and needs about ten rounds instead of a chain's length. Its result is not the one of a loop in index order, so the host engine must then implement the same selection rule if host and device are to give the same model.

4c. Chains: pointer jumping and list ranking. Read first-hand only Polak, Siwiec, Wozniak, "Euler Meets GPU" (arXiv 2103.15217, sections 2.2, 3.1): they use the list ranking of Wei and JaJa because it "performs much better than the classical pointer jumping technique", and plain pointer jumping (five jumps per kernel before a global synchronisation) for node levels, where it "is already fast enough never to be a bottleneck". From search summaries only, unchecked: Rehman, Kothapalli, Narayanan (ICS 2009) report that pointer jumping beat a CPU only from about half a million list elements and that their recursive scheme ranks 32 million elements in about a second. My inference: pointer jumping over the alias forest is synchronous and therefore deterministic, but it composes the affine maps x = a*y + b in a different association than a host that follows the chain, so the coefficients can differ in the last bits; jumping on indices only (root and depth) and composing level by level from the root gives one association order on both engines.

4d. Parallel rows and columns by hashing and sorting. Sources: 1 (PaPILO), 3a, 3b, and HiGHS (section 5). All use a hash of the support and of scaled coefficients, a grouping (sort or hash table) and an exact test inside a group. PaPILO and cuPSLP test against one leader per group, which avoids chains of nearly parallel rows. The engine's key (rules_parallel_rows.cpp lines 28-110) is a sum of per-entry hashes of (column, coefficient scaled by the entry of the smallest column, rounded to 20 mantissa bits), so it does not depend on storage order and is an integer reduction per row, exact on a device. Gemander, Chen, Weninger, Gottwald, Gleixner, Martin, "Two-row and two-column mixed-integer presolve using hashing-based pairing methods" (2020): title and abstract only.

4e. Removing rows and columns on a device. cuPSLP keeps flags and never compacts during presolve; GPU-Preprocessor keeps masks and rebuilds both orientations once per batch. The project's own figures (Stage 0 report): a stable radix sort rebuilds the CSC in 467 microseconds + 0.279 ns per nonzero, compaction after deletions only costs 0.70 times that, and one CPU thread is faster on 4 of the 6 matrices up to 100,933 nonzeros.

4f. Dynamic sparse matrices on a GPU (Hornet, faimGraph, Awad et al. "Dynamic Graphs on the GPU"): search summaries only, unchecked. They serve streams of edge insertions with per-vertex blocks or hash tables. Neither GPU presolver uses one. Stage 1 has little fill-in (row addition, substitution of doubleton equations), so I see no case for them; this is my inference.

4g. Sums with a fixed order. NVIDIA CCCL 3.1 (developer blog "Controlling floating-point determinism in NVIDIA CCCL" and the CUB determinism page): cub::DeviceReduce has three levels: not_guaranteed (atomics, one kernel), run_to_run (default, fixed tree, same bits on the same GPU with the same build), gpu_to_gpu (a reproducible accumulator with exponent bins, 20 to 30% slower on large inputs). cub::DeviceSegmentedReduce supports not_guaranteed and run_to_run only; DeviceScan defaults to not_guaranteed. So no library reduction gives a per-row floating-point sum that is the same on every GPU type; the row sums need the project's own kernel with a tree fixed by entry position (DESIGN.md 2.4, lane groups), and library reductions stay for integers, minimum and maximum, as DESIGN.md 2.5 already says. Reproducible summation of Demmel, Ahrens, Nguyen (ReproBLAS: order-independent, about 7n additions): search summary only.

Cautions for batch application that follow (my inference)
- Lock-based dual fixing, empty and redundant rows, and bound changes combined by maximum and minimum can be applied together: each proof holds for every value of the other variables.
- A proof that reads an implied bound has premises on the source row and on every column bound that row's activity used. Two such proofs can lean on each other; a batch needs the premise check of section 1 or a reservation of those lines. This covers the free and implied-free singleton column, the forcing column, dominated columns and dual bound strengthening.
- Choices by "current column length" or "first in the bucket" must become functions of the frozen state (length at batch start, smallest index), or host and device differ.
- Stop tests on "percent removed" must count the same things on both engines.

7. RESULTS THAT SPEAK AGAINST A GPU FOR A PART OF THE CASCADE

1. The cascade tail. Sofranac et al. section 5: after single bound changes the marked sequential code is often faster. Progress paper: the speedup drops steeply in the last percent before the fixed point. Local: later calls are about 10% of the host time (240 instances, estimate), the median call of every family but the row rules finds nothing or almost nothing, and unitcal_7 spends 24 microseconds of host time per family call, less than one device primitive.
2. Rounds. A Jacobi sweep needs 1.4 times the rounds on average and up to 22 times (893 instances); PaPILO's delayed application needs 23.5 instead of 14.5 rounds (990 instances). Each extra round costs the fixed device cost of every family in it.
3. Small models. Sofranac et al.: 2.35 times on the 270 smallest instances on a V100 without transfers, and a small GPU (P400) is slower than the CPU on every size class. PaPILO: 1,617 of 2,044 runs take under a second and the gain over all runs is 1.9 times at 32 threads. Local: the device state build loses below 8.5e5 nonzeros as a first call, and 50 instances between 5e4 and 2e5 nonzeros take 15 ms in the median on the host for the whole presolve.
4. Sequential work on the device. cuPSLP 2.2: one GPU thread is about 1,000 times slower than a CPU core on a sum of 2.4 million numbers. Any chain that is walked by one thread (a long alias chain, a singleton cascade, a hash chain) belongs on the host. The model hash of today (hash.cpp lines 34-48) is such a chain: each word is mixed into the previous value, so it cannot be computed in parallel as defined.
5. Rules that collide with their own kind. PaPILO: singleton columns 27.7% conflicts with themselves, doubleton equations 17.4% discarded, dominated columns 36.5% discarded (240 benchmark instances). A batch on a frozen state loses that share to the next round, and the median batch is tiny (table of section 6: singleton columns 25.5 findings per call at the 90th percentile).
6. Checks that are too cheap. PaPILO 2.5 does not parallelise simple probing over all constraints because the checks are very fast.
7. Determinism has a price that the published GPU presolvers did not pay. Both use floating-point atomics (cuPSLP for bounds, GPU-Preprocessor for row sides); Sofranac et al. use atomic maximum and minimum on doubles; CCCL's GPU-to-GPU level costs 20 to 30% and does not exist for segmented sums; the fixed reduction order of Kempke et al. cost a factor of about 6 on five instances. Deterministic reservations cost 1.56 and 2.27 times on one thread in Blelloch et al.
8. Linearly dependent equations: called inherently hard to parallelise by cuPSLP section 5 (not a Stage 1 rule, named for completeness).
9. The first assumption of the PSLP authors (a GPU presolve gains little) was wrong for large LPs, so item 3 is about size, not about presolve as such.

8. WHAT NOBODY SEEMS TO HAVE DONE (within what I found)

- A GPU presolve with MIP rules: coefficient tightening, rounding of integer bounds inside propagation, dual fixing and substitution with integrality conditions, merging of parallel integer columns, implied integers, simple probing. Both GPU presolvers are for LP and are tested on LP relaxations only; Sofranac et al. cover propagation only.
- A GPU presolve that is reproducible bit for bit, across runs, GPU types and against a host engine. No GPU source states it; all use floating-point atomics or compare with tolerances.
- Compensated row activities with one summation order shared by a host and a device engine.
- A parallel apply phase with a stated conflict rule. PaPILO applies sequentially; cuPSLP is silent; GPU-Preprocessor names only "equations that do not share variables" for doubleton equations.
- A batch whose result equals the sequential loop in a fixed order (internal determinism in the sense of Blelloch et al.) for presolve reductions. PaPILO is deterministic but its batch result differs from its sequential mode.
- Chains of aliases resolved on a device (pointer jumping over an alias forest). GPU-Preprocessor avoids chains by taking variable-disjoint equations per batch.
- A host/device split inside one presolve call with thresholds by work. cuPSLP and GPU-Preprocessor run everything on the device and exclude transfers from their timings; cuPSLP proposes a hybrid only for dependent equations.
- Postsolve records produced on a device in a defined order (cuPSLP keeps a stack on the device without saying how its order is fixed).
- Unified memory on Grace Hopper in a presolve: no source mentions it.
- A random-model oracle or wrong-engine campaign for a GPU presolve.
